activities.anchor: Nothing in the data forces the choice
activities.caption: naming the direction — pair each role with its clause
activities.name: ciVarMatch

config.prompt: Match each role or regression to what it asserts:

pairs.right: the suspected driver — plotted on the horizontal axis
the response — plotted on the vertical axis

pairs.left: regressing revision hours on exam score
pairs.right: 'given five hours of practice, what score should we expect?'
'given a score of 70, how much practice is typical?' — a genuinely different quantity, not a rounding of the first

config.why: The least-squares line of y on x is not the algebraic inverse of the line of x on y — each answers a different conditional question.

activities.anchor: the direction of causation can be read off the scatter
activities.caption: what the plot records vs what supplies the arrow — drag the divider
activities.name: ciDirCompare

config.prompt: The same 200 points, two claims — drag the divider:

before.label: what the scatter records
before.text: correlation of 0.9 in either direction — association, identical whichever arrow you draw

after.label: what supplies the direction
after.text: time ordering, experiment design or a defensible causal argument — x causing y, y causing x, or a third variable causing both

config.why: Strength of association is not a direction-finder; the diagram only records the association.

activities.caption: r ≈ 0, yet perfectly deterministic — which curve?
activities.name: ciCurveTrace

config.prompt: The relationship is deterministic but r is essentially 0 — which curve is it?

curves.label: a symmetric curve — no linear pattern at all

config.why: r = 0 does not certify independence — it certifies only the absence of a linear pattern; curvature, clusters, gaps and outliers are invisible to a single number.

activities.anchor: a lower half and an upper half
activities.caption: the semi-averages method, in order
activities.name: ciSemiOrder

config.prompt: Fit the line by semi-averages — order the steps:
items: Order the points by x, then split into lower and upper halves
Compute the mean of x and the mean of y in each half — (2.5, 20) and (6.5, 45) in the worked set
Draw the unique straight line through those two mean points
Read the slope: (45 − 20) ÷ (6.5 − 2.5) = 6.25 wpm per hour
config.why: A one-pass prototype of least squares — and robust to a single wild point in a way naive eyeballing is not.

activities.anchor: minimises the sum of squared vertical distances
activities.caption: one line of this fitted-line anatomy is wrong — click it
activities.name: ciLineSpot

config.prompt: One line of this fitted-line anatomy is wrong — click it:
lines: Slope b = r × (sy ÷ sx): 0.80 × (10 ÷ 5) = 1.6 points per hour.
Intercept a = mean of y − b × mean of x: 70 − 1.6 × 12 = 50.8.
The slope is a claim about each individual student — 1.6 points for this student.
R² = 0.64: hours account for 64% of the variance, leaving 36% — precisely where confounding enters.
config.correction: The slope is a claim about average effect within the observed range — 1.6 points per hour on average, never 1.6 for this student.
config.why: The line explains variation, not persons — the slope is an anatomy of averages.

activities.anchor: which may be outside the data
activities.caption: true or false — the intercept's meaning
activities.name: ciIntJudge

statements.why: It is the prediction at x = 0 — which may be outside the data (nobody revised for 0 hours here and sat the exam) or meaningless (zero height).

statements.s: Here the intercept 50.8 is the predicted score with zero revision.
statements.why: That is what it computes — but zero revision hours is an x value the data never contains.

statements.s: Interpret the intercept only where the data actually lives.
statements.why: Report it, but read it only inside the observed range.

activities.anchor: Shoe size against age fits beautifully
activities.caption: export the fit past its range — what shoe size?
activities.name: ciShoeEst

config.prompt: Shoe size against age fits ages 3 to 10 beautifully. Extrapolated to age 25, it predicts what size?
config.why: Size 17 — the true relationship levels off where the data ends. Extrapolation fails categorically, not gradually.
config.context: An extrapolation of 10% past the range is an estimate; 50% past it is a hope; past a known turning point it is wrong by construction.

activities.caption: the diagrams' verdict — control, or never control?
activities.name: ciDagSort

config.prompt: Pearl's rules are unforgiving — file each variable:

items.label: a confounder — a common cause of treatment and outcome
a mediator — part of the effect you would erase
a collider — a variable caused by two others

config.why: Conditioning on a collider manufactures association from nothing — among movie stars, beauty and talent appear negatively correlated because stardom requires at least one of the two.
